To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the density dependence of the meson masses, as proposed in many previous works, is essential for a consistent interpretation of the experimental data in the several hundred megaelectronvolt region.

1) the introduction of a density dependent nucleon mass in a nonlocal optical model potential removes the radius discrepancy which has persisted in analyses with the conventional nonrelativistic IA; 2) the nonlocality of this potential is consistent with earlier calculations; 3) the density dependent masses aid in increasing spin-orbit strength; 4) a relativistic IA2 calculation of spin observables shows a large spin-orbit splitting and a strong polarization in the 200 MeV region
the density dependent meson-nucleon coupling constants are necessary to remove the radius discrepancy and to improve the agreement of the optical model calculations with experiment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new method of describing the nucleon-nucleus optical potential in terms of a relativistic many-body approach.
the problem of the nuclear density dependence of the meson-nucleon coupling constants in the nucleus.
the problem of the nuclear density dependence of the effective meson-nucleon mass and its effect on the proton-nucleus optical potential in the several hundred-MeV region.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the introduction of the density dependent meson mass is a very promising approach for the description of the nucleon-nucleus optical potential and its spin-orbit part.
the inclusion of density dependent masses in a relativistic IA2 model gives a very good description of all the available proton-nucleus elastic scattering data in the 200-500 MeV range.
the density dependence of the meson masses is required to explain the proton scattering data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the density dependent meson-nucleon couplings provide a reasonable framework for describing the nucleon-nucleus interaction.
the density dependence of the meson masses is essential to obtain a satisfactory description of proton-nucleus data in the 200-400 MeV region.
the density dependent meson mass is a necessary ingredient in the IA2 formalism for the description of nucleon-nucleus scattering at energies below the pion production threshold.
The main takeaway from our work is that
density-dependent meson masses, as well as other relativistic corrections, are needed for a proper description of proton-nucleus elastic scattering.
density dependent meson mass models, with the correct range of nonlocalities, can explain the nuclear radius discrepancy and improve the description of proton scattering from nuclei.
the relativistic impulse approximation is a viable approach to describe proton-nucleus elastic scattering at intermediate energies.
